items.lessonTitle: In the beginning, Being alone (6.2)

neighbors.heading: one stuff under everything
neighbors.text: Today Uddalaka said that in the beginning there was Being alone, one without a second. Philosophers have reached for the same oneness. Baruch Spinoza wrote: "Besides God no substance can be granted or conceived." For him, the chair, the tree and your own hand are all ways the one substance shows itself, which he also called Nature.
neighbors.difference: Uddalaka's Being thinks, let me be many, and sends out heat, water and food. Spinoza's God, or Nature, doesn't choose or wish; everything follows from its nature, the way a triangle's angles follow from being a triangle.
neighbors.shared: under all the different names, one thing holds everything together.
neighbors.sources: Spinoza, Ethics, Part I, Proposition 14 (Elwes translation, 1883)

neighbors.heading: one, without a second
neighbors.text: Today Uddalaka said that in the beginning there was Being alone, one only, without a second. Jews say a line about oneness morning and night: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." And the Torah opens at the very same moment: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."
neighbors.difference: In Uddalaka's telling, Being itself grows forth into heat, water and food. In Genesis, God speaks the world into being: made by God, and distinct from him.
neighbors.shared: the whole wide world begins from one.

items.lessonTitle: The salt in water — "taste it here. here. everywhere." (6.13)

neighbors.heading: in every sip
neighbors.text: Today the salt vanished into the water, and still every sip was salty. Christians speak of a God that close. Paul told the people of Athens that God is "not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being." And a psalm asks: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit?"
neighbors.difference: Uddalaka ends with tat tvam asi, you are that, and Hindu schools read it as oneness or as close belonging. For Christians, God is everywhere and holds you up, yet you stay a creature he loves.
neighbors.shared: what matters most is close, even when you can't see it.

neighbors.heading: wherever you turn
neighbors.text: Today the salt vanished into the water, and still every sip was salty. The Qur'an speaks of a nearness like that: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." And of each person: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."
neighbors.difference: Uddalaka says of the hidden essence: you are that. Muslims hold that Allah is nearer than your own vein, yet beyond everything he created; no creature shares his being.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for is closer than you think.

items.lessonTitle: The city of Brahman in the heart (8.1)

neighbors.heading: a castle inside
neighbors.text: Today the Upanishad found a small space in the heart, as big as the sky outside. Catholics look inward too. Jesus says in the Gospel: "For lo, the kingdom of God is within you." And Saint Teresa of Avila pictured the soul as a castle of clear crystal with many rooms, and God living in the room at the very center.
neighbors.difference: For the Upanishad, what lives in the heart's space is the self that never ages or dies. For Catholics, God dwells in the soul by grace, as a guest and friend; the soul, however beautiful, is made.
neighbors.shared: the biggest room you'll ever find is inside you.
neighbors.sources: Luke 17:21 (Douay-Rheims) · Teresa of Avila, The Interior Castle, First Mansions, ch. 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today the Upanishad found a small space in the heart that holds heaven and earth. Guru Tegh Bahadur asks a seeker why he goes looking in the forest: the Lord dwells in everything, untouched, and stays right there with you. Again and again the Guru Granth Sahib sings that the One you seek is found within.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad draws a map: body, lotus-house, inner space. Sikhs keep no map like that. The One is formless and everywhere, met within by remembering the Name and living the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to travel far to find what you're seeking.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Guru Tegh Bahadur (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: The gods and demons and the breath (1.3)

neighbors.heading: the breath that stays clean
neighbors.text: Today speech, sight, hearing and mind were all pierced, and only the plain breath stayed clean. Jewish mornings start with a similar hope. The Talmud gives a prayer for waking: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure; you created it, you breathed it into me. In Hebrew, the word for soul, neshamah, is close kin to the word for breath.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, breath stays clean because it took nothing for itself. In the Jewish prayer, the soul is pure because God made it so, and each morning begins with thanks for it.
neighbors.shared: something in you stayed clean, whatever the day has done.

neighbors.heading: the bright mind
neighbors.text: Today the demons pierced speech, sight, hearing and mind, but broke on the plain breath like clay on stone. The Buddha points to something clear underneath too. In a short teaching he says the mind is luminous, and gets stained by troubles that arrive from outside. And his breathing meditation starts simply: breathe in knowing it, breathe out knowing it.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad's breath wins because it grabs nothing, and carries the senses past death. The Buddha's bright mind isn't a lasting self; it's a mind that can be cleared, moment by moment, through practice.
neighbors.shared: under the noise, there's something clear you can come back to.
neighbors.sources: Anguttara Nikaya 1.49–52 (paraphrase) · Anapanasati Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 118 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Maitreyi: "what would I do with wealth if it doesn't make me immortal?" (2.4)

neighbors.heading: what lasts
neighbors.text: Today Maitreyi was offered a share of the property and asked: what would I do with something that won't make me deathless? The Qur'an weighs wealth the same way: "Wealth and children are an ornament of life of the world. But the good deeds which endure are better in thy Lord's sight for reward, and better in respect of hope."
neighbors.difference: Maitreyi asks for knowledge of the self, the thing that doesn't end. The Qur'an points to good deeds that endure, carried before Allah, with hope in his mercy in the life to come.
neighbors.shared: money is fine; just don't let it answer the wrong question.

neighbors.heading: care for the soul
neighbors.text: Today Maitreyi set the money aside and asked for what doesn't end. Socrates, on trial for his life in Athens, asked his city the same kind of question: aren't you ashamed to care so much about money, reputation and honor, and so little about wisdom, truth, and making your soul as good as it can be?
neighbors.difference: Maitreyi wants the deathless, and asks a teacher for it. Socrates asks every citizen to care for the soul right now, and admits he doesn't know for certain what death brings.
neighbors.shared: the best question is often the one underneath the offer.

items.lessonTitle: Uddalaka: the thread and the inner controller (3.7)

neighbors.heading: the knower within
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya named the inner controller, who lives in the earth, the wind and your breath, and rules each from within. Sikhs call the One Antarjami, the knower within every heart, a name the Guru Granth Sahib uses again and again. And the Japji says everyone is within the Hukam, the divine order; no one stands outside it.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the inner controller is your own self, the deathless. Sikhs speak of the Creator dwelling in all, never born, and the path is living in tune with the Hukam by remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: a quiet thread runs through everything, including you.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji pauri 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the thread through the beads
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya said a thread holds this world and the next together, like a string through beads, and an inner controller rules each thing from within. Christians say something like it of Christ. Paul writes: "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist." To consist here means to hold together.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the inner controller is called your self, the deathless. Christians say all things hold together in Christ, the Son through whom God made the world, while each person stays a creature God loves.
neighbors.shared: you're held together by more than you can see.

items.lessonTitle: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man? sun → moon → fire → speech → self (4.3)

neighbors.heading: a lamp for yourself
neighbors.text: Today the sun set, the moon set, the fire went out, speech fell silent, and the self was left as a person's own light. Near the end of his life, the Buddha told his friends not to lean on him once he was gone: be a lamp, an island, for yourselves, with the teaching as your lamp and refuge.
neighbors.difference: Yajnavalkya's light is the self made of knowing, the light within the heart. The Buddha's lamp isn't a lasting self; it's your own effort and the teaching, lit again each day.
neighbors.shared: when the other lights go out, you aren't left in the dark.

neighbors.heading: the light in everyone
neighbors.text: Today, with sun, moon, fire and voice all gone, Yajnavalkya said the self is a person's own light. Catholics speak of a light no night puts out. Saint John's Gospel says of Christ: "That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world." And Jesus tells his friends: "You are the light of the world."
neighbors.difference: For Yajnavalkya, the light is the self itself. For Catholics, the true light is Christ, God's Word, shining into each person from beyond them; we carry it like a lamp, not as its source.
neighbors.shared: there's a light in you that the dark doesn't reach.

items.lessonTitle: "As is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed" (4.4)

neighbors.heading: you become what you do
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya said: as a person acts, so they become; doing good, one becomes good. Aristotle said the same about character: "we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts." Psychologists today call the pattern habit: what you repeat gets easier, and slowly turns into who you are.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle starts with practice and says the right wanting grows from it. Yajnavalkya looks one step further back, to desire itself, and follows the chain past death into the next life.
neighbors.shared: small choices, repeated, quietly build a person.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (W. D. Ross translation)

neighbors.heading: one good deed pulls the next
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya traced a chain: desire to will, will to deed, deed to what you become. The Mishnah has a chain too. Ben Azzai taught: run to do even a small commandment, and flee from wrongdoing, because one good deed pulls another after it, and one wrong pulls another. The reward of a good deed is the next good deed.
neighbors.difference: Yajnavalkya follows the chain past death into another life, unless desire for the self ends it. Ben Azzai speaks of commandments given by God, done in this life, with the reward left in God's hands.
neighbors.shared: every good thing you do makes the next one easier.

items.lessonTitle: "Do not despise food. Food is Brahman." (3.7–3.10)

neighbors.heading: nothing to be refused
neighbors.text: Today the Taittiriya said: do not despise food; that is the vow. Christians honor food with thanks. Paul writes: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer." That's one reason Christian families pause to say grace before eating.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad calls food Brahman: the chain of eating and being eaten is the holy itself. Christians call food a good gift from God, made holy by thanks, while the Giver stays other than the gift.
neighbors.shared: the plate in front of you deserves a moment of thanks.

neighbors.heading: he never faulted a meal
neighbors.text: Today the Taittiriya said: do not despise food, and never turn away a guest. Muslims remember the same manners in the Prophet. His companion Abu Hurairah said the Prophet never found fault with any food: if he liked it, he ate it, and if not, he left it. The Qur'an adds: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal."
neighbors.difference: For the Upanishad, food is Brahman, the very chain of life. For Muslims, food is rizq, provision from Allah, begun with his name and ended with thanks; the gift is never the Giver.
neighbors.shared: food is a gift; no meal is beneath a thank you.

items.lessonTitle: The person; the gods enter through the doors of the body (1.2)

neighbors.heading: a temple, well made
neighbors.text: Today the gods turned down a cow and a horse, saw a human being and said: well made, indeed! Catholics honor the body too. Genesis says God saw all he had made, "and they were very good." And Saint Paul asks: "know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is in you?"
neighbors.difference: In the Aitareya, many gods move in: fire as speech, the sun as sight. Catholics believe in one God, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in the baptized, so the body is honored as his temple.
neighbors.shared: your body isn't a burden; it's a good home.

neighbors.heading: the body the gods long for
neighbors.text: Today the gods saw a human being and said: well made, indeed! Bhagat Kabir sings something close in the Guru Granth Sahib: even the gods long for this human body, so use it to serve and remember the Lord. Guru Amar Das calls the body the Lord's temple, where the jewel of wisdom comes to light.
neighbors.difference: In the Aitareya, the gods move in and become speech, breath and sight. Sikhs worship the One alone; for them, a human birth is a rare chance to meet that One by remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: this body is a gift worth taking good care of.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Bhagat Kabir (paraphrase) · Ang 1346, Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Rituals are leaky boats (1.2)

neighbors.heading: more than offerings
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka praised the fire rites as true, then called them unsteady boats. Israel's prophets made a similar turn. Through Hosea, God says: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt-offerings." The offerings were commanded and kept, and still the prophets kept asking what they were for.
neighbors.difference: The Mundaka says rites win a heaven that runs out, so the seeker looks past them to the imperishable. Hosea doesn't set the commandments aside; he asks that kindness and knowing God fill them.
neighbors.shared: a ritual is a boat; remember where it's taking you.

neighbors.heading: a raft, not a home
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka called the rites unsteady boats. The Buddha told a boat story too. A traveler builds a raft to cross a flood. On the far shore, should he carry it on his head? No. The teaching, the Buddha said, is like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding onto.
neighbors.difference: The Mundaka honors the Vedic rites, then points past them to the imperishable. The Buddha counted clinging to rites and rituals among the fetters, and said even his own teaching is a raft to set down.
neighbors.shared: the boat matters; so does knowing when you've reached the shore.

items.lessonTitle: "Truth alone prevails" — satyam eva jayate (3.1)

neighbors.heading: truth has come
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka said: truth alone wins, not untruth. The Qur'an says it just as plainly: "Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away. Lo! falsehood is ever bound to vanish." And one of Allah's names is al-Haqq, the Truth: "That is because Allah, He is the Truth."
neighbors.difference: In the Mundaka, satya comes from sat, what is, and truth is a road the sages walk. In Islam, the Truth is a name of Allah himself, and falsehood can't stand before him.
neighbors.shared: what's crooked doesn't last; what's true holds.

neighbors.heading: the long arc
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka said truth alone wins, and lays the road the sages walk. In 1853 the American minister Theodore Parker said something like it about justice: he couldn't see the whole moral universe, and the arc is long, but from what he could see, he was sure it bends toward justice. Martin Luther King Jr. later made the line famous.
neighbors.difference: The Mundaka sets truth inside the right order of things, and makes it a road to the self. Parker spoke from conscience and the long view of history, without claiming to know how it works.
neighbors.shared: truth can take its time; it still gets there.
neighbors.sources: Theodore Parker, "Of Justice and the Conscience," Ten Sermons of Religion (1853) (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Rudra — the one god (3.1–3.4)

neighbors.heading: there is One
neighbors.text: Today the Shvetashvatara said: Rudra is truly one; they do not stand for a second. The Guru Granth Sahib opens on the same number. Its first word is Ik Onkar: there is One. Guru Nanak's Mool Mantar goes on to describe that One: true name, creator, without fear, without hate, beyond time, never born, self-existent.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad gives the One a name from the old hymns, Rudra, whom Shaiva readers worship as Shiva. Sikhs speak of the One as formless and never born, called by many names, belonging to no single story.
neighbors.shared: you can turn toward the One in your own words.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the Lord is one
neighbors.text: Today the Shvetashvatara said Rudra is one, ruling every world from within. Asked which commandment comes first, Jesus quoted Israel's great prayer, the Shema: "Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart." Christians call him the maker of heaven and earth, near to every creature.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad gives the one Lord a face and a name, Rudra, later loved as Shiva. Christians believe the one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and came close in Jesus.
neighbors.shared: the One who made the stars still turns toward you.

items.lessonTitle: "Now, yoga." Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind (1.1–1.2)

neighbors.heading: straightening the arrow
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali defined yoga as the stilling of the turnings of the mind. The Buddha watched the same whirl. The Dhammapada says: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back." The next verse compares the mind to a fish flapping on dry land.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali stills the mind so the seer can rest in its own nature. The Buddha trains the mind toward freedom without pointing to a lasting seer behind it.
neighbors.shared: a busy mind can learn to settle, a little at a time.

neighbors.heading: be still
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Catholics pray a psalm that asks for stillness too: "Be still and see that I am God." Monks and nuns have kept that quiet for centuries, and Catholics today may sit in silent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, simply resting in God's presence.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's stillness lets the seer rest in itself, and no god is named yet. In Catholic prayer, the stillness is for meeting God, who is other than you and comes to you as a friend.
neighbors.shared: when the stirring settles, something deeper can be seen.

items.lessonTitle: Friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity (1.33)

neighbors.heading: the people you'll meet today
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali gave four keys: friendliness, compassion, gladness, and calm toward those who do wrong. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius practiced the fourth. One morning note to himself reads: today I'll meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant. They can't truly harm me, and I won't be angry with them, because we were made to work together, like two hands.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali offers the four attitudes to clear and settle the mind on the way to stillness. Marcus reasons as a Stoic: all people share one reason, so anger at them is like a hand fighting a foot.
neighbors.shared: how you meet people shapes the mind you carry home.

neighbors.heading: don't cheer when they fall
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali paired four attitudes with four kinds of people, and the hardest was calm toward those who do wrong. Proverbs asks the same: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thy heart be glad when he stumbleth." And in the Mishnah, Shammai adds a gentler one: greet every person with a cheerful face.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali offers the four keys to make the mind clear and calm. Proverbs grounds it in God: gloating over an enemy displeases the LORD. Jewish teachers add that every person is made in God's image.
neighbors.shared: kindness toward people steadies your own heart.

items.lessonTitle: Kriya yoga — discipline, study, surrender (2.1–2.2)

neighbors.heading: thy will be done
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named the third part of the yoga of action: surrender to the Lord, offering your actions and letting go of their fruits. The night before he died, Jesus prayed in a garden: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Christians pray it in the Lord's Prayer: "Thy will be done."
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's Ishvara is a special self, the first teacher, untouched by affliction, and surrender thins the mind's knots. For Christians, surrender is trust in a loving Father, following Jesus, who did it first.
neighbors.shared: you can do your best and then open your hands.

neighbors.heading: the one who surrenders
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named surrender to the Lord as part of everyday yoga. In Arabic, the word islam itself means surrender, and a muslim is one who surrenders. The Qur'an says: "Nay, but whosoever surrendereth his purpose to Allah while doing good, his reward is with his Lord; and there shall no fear come upon them neither shall they grieve."
neighbors.difference: In the Yoga Sutras, surrender is one practice among three, a way to thin the afflictions. In Islam, surrender to Allah, the One, is the whole of the faith, lived through prayer, fasting and doing good.
neighbors.shared: giving your effort away makes it lighter to carry.

items.lessonTitle: Ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent (2.4–2.5)

neighbors.heading: what is seen, what is not
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named the first mix-up: taking the passing for the permanent. Saint Paul keeps his eyes on the same difference: "we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen, are temporal; but the things which are not seen, are eternal."
neighbors.difference: For Patanjali, the deepest mix-up is taking the body and mind for the self, the seer. For Catholics, passing things are still God's good gifts; what lasts is God, and the life he promises.
neighbors.shared: hold the passing things gently; they were never meant to last.

neighbors.heading: whatever is made will pass
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named the root mix-up: taking what passes for what lasts. Guru Tegh Bahadur says it in his closing verses in the Guru Granth Sahib: whatever has come into being will pass away, today or tomorrow. And he names what stays: the Name stays, the saints stay, the Guru stays.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's cure is discernment: telling the seer apart from what it sees. The Guru's cure is singing the praises of the One and remembering the Name, which doesn't pass.
neighbors.shared: everything passes, and something worth holding stays.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Yama — non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint, non-grasping (2.30–2.31)

neighbors.heading: five, and ten
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named five restraints: non-harm, truthfulness, not stealing, restraint, not grasping. Several will sound familiar from Sinai: "Thou shalt not murder. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." And the last commandment goes inside, like not grasping: "Thou shalt not covet."
neighbors.difference: Patanjali puts non-harm first, as the root of the rest, and makes the five the first limb toward stillness. The Ten Commandments come as God's covenant with Israel, and begin with God before turning to neighbors.
neighbors.shared: a good life starts with how you treat the people around you.

neighbors.heading: the five precepts
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named five restraints, with non-harm first. Buddhists take five precepts, and they rhyme almost line for line: I undertake to refrain from killing living beings, from taking what isn't given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from drink and drugs that cloud the mind. Buddhists recite them at a temple or at home.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's fifth is not grasping; the Buddhist fifth is a clear head, free of intoxicants. Buddhists take the precepts as training steps toward awakening; Patanjali calls the five, kept without exception, the great vow.
neighbors.shared: do no harm is a good first step on any path.
neighbors.sources: The five precepts (pañcasīla), as recited in Pali (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Concentration, meditation, absorption (3.1–3.3)

neighbors.heading: a heart at prayer
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said concentration is binding the mind to one place: it slips, you bring it back. Muslims call the heart's focus in prayer khushu'. The Qur'an opens a chapter with it: "Successful indeed are the believers / Who are humble in their prayers." Teachers say: let the eyes rest on the place of prostration, and the heart on Allah.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's concentration can rest on any one place, the navel, the heart, the tip of the nose, and leads toward absorption. In Islam, the focus is turning the whole heart to Allah in the daily prayers.
neighbors.shared: each time the mind wanders, you can gently bring it back.

neighbors.heading: bringing it back
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali defined concentration as holding the mind on one place, and bringing it back each time it slips. The psychologist William James wrote: "the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." An education that trained it, he said, would be the best education there is.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali trains attention as a step toward samadhi, where the sense of me drops away. James studied attention as a scientist, for clearer thinking and a steadier will, without a goal beyond the mind.
neighbors.shared: the coming back is the practice, not the failure.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 11

items.lessonTitle: The powers are obstacles to samadhi (3.37)

neighbors.heading: other tastes
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali turned the list of powers over: seen from samadhi, they're obstacles. Guru Nanak said something close to the wonder-working yogis of his day. In the Japji he sings that the Lord is the true master who holds everything together, and miraculous powers are other tastes, flavors that pull you away from him.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali doesn't call the powers false; he keeps them in their place on the way to freedom. Guru Nanak sets them aside for something sweeter: the Name, and living in the Hukam.
neighbors.shared: the flashy gift isn't the treasure; keep your eyes on what matters.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji pauri 29 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: and have not love
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said the powers are obstacles if the goal is stillness. Saint Paul says gifts can miss the point too: "And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing."
neighbors.difference: For Patanjali, the powers distract from resting as the seer. For Paul, the greatest gift is love, God's own love living in us; without it, even miracles are empty.
neighbors.shared: the most impressive thing isn't always the most important.

items.lessonTitle: Kaivalya — when purity of mind equals purity of self (3.55–3.56)

neighbors.heading: purify the mind
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said freedom comes when the mind is as clear as the seer: wipe the glass until it adds nothing. The Dhammapada sums up the teaching in one short verse: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's seer never needed cleaning; only the mind does. The Buddha points to no seer behind it: purifying the mind ends craving, and that ending is itself freedom.
neighbors.shared: clearing the mind is quiet work, and worth it.

neighbors.heading: the clean of heart
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said freedom comes when the mind is wiped as clean as the seer. Jesus promises something like it in the Beatitudes: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." Catholics speak of purity of heart as a lifelong work of grace: confession, prayer, and letting go of whatever clouds the way we see.
neighbors.difference: For Patanjali, a clean mind lets the seer stand alone, needing nothing. For Catholics, a clean heart is God's gift, and its reward is seeing God face to face, in love.
neighbors.shared: a clear heart sees more truly.

items.lessonTitle: Valmiki and Narada

neighbors.heading: looking for a person
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki asked: is there anyone alive who is truthful, kind, grateful, and has conquered anger? A Greek philosopher asked it his own way. Diogenes, the story goes, walked about in broad daylight holding a lit lamp, and told anyone who asked that he was looking for a human being, a real one.
neighbors.difference: Narada answers Valmiki with a name, Rama, and the whole epic becomes the evidence. Diogenes' lamp was a joke with a point: he never claimed to find anyone.
neighbors.shared: good character is rare, and worth looking for.
neighbors.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: be the one
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki asked if anyone alive held all sixteen good qualities, and Narada said they're hard to find together. Hillel turned the search around. In the Mishnah he teaches: in a place where there are no worthy people, try to be one yourself. His word is ish, a person who stands up when it counts.
neighbors.difference: Narada names Rama, and the epic tells his story as the answer. Hillel names no hero; he hands the question back to the listener, to be lived out under God's commandments.
neighbors.shared: if you can't find the good person, start becoming one.

items.lessonTitle: Dasharatha's sacrifice

neighbors.heading: thy prayer is heard
neighbors.text: Today Dasharatha, the king who had everything but a son, told his counselors his grief and asked for help. Luke's Gospel opens with an old priest, Zacharias, and his wife Elisabeth, who had no child either. While he served in the Temple, an angel said: "Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."
neighbors.difference: Dasharatha's sons come through a great sacrifice, and one of them is Vishnu born as a man. Zacharias's son is John the Baptist, a prophet sent to prepare the way for Jesus.
neighbors.shared: it's brave to say out loud what you're longing for.

neighbors.heading: the old man's prayer
neighbors.text: Today Dasharatha admitted the one thing he lacked, a son, and asked for help. The Qur'an tells of Zakariyya praying in secret: "My Lord! Lo! the bones of me wax feeble and my head is shining with grey hair, and I have never been unblest in prayer to Thee, my Lord." And Allah gives him good news of a son, Yahya.
neighbors.difference: Dasharatha seeks sons through a great royal sacrifice with priests and counselors. Zakariyya simply calls on his Lord, alone and in secret; his son Yahya is a prophet and a servant of Allah.
neighbors.shared: an honest ask can open a door you thought was shut.

items.lessonTitle: Tataka

neighbors.heading: no more force than needed
neighbors.text: Today Rama tried the gentlest way first: take away her power to harm, not her life. Catholic teaching sets the same limit on defending yourself. Following Saint Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says you may repel force to protect yourself and others, but if you use more violence than is necessary, it becomes wrong.
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana, the sage finally urges Rama to finish the fight, and the forest is freed. Catholic teaching asks that force be measured, used only as far as defense requires.
neighbors.shared: even when you must stand firm, choose the gentlest way that works.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2264, citing Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, 64, 7 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the last resort
neighbors.text: Today Rama tried to disarm Tataka before anything harder. Guru Gobind Singh wrote to the emperor Aurangzeb in a Persian letter, the Zafarnama: when every other way has been tried and has failed, then it is right to take up the sword. Sikhs honor the saint-soldier: gentle first, brave when there's no other choice.
neighbors.difference: Rama acts as a prince protecting a sage's rite, at his teacher's word. The Guru speaks of defending the wronged against broken promises, and only after every peaceful means has run out.
neighbors.shared: strength is best when gentleness has had its turn first.
neighbors.sources: Zafarnama of Guru Gobind Singh, verse 22 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: the four weddings

neighbors.heading: a help beside him
neighbors.text: Today Janaka gave Sita to Rama as sahadharmachari, one who walks the path of dharma together with you. The Torah begins marriage with loneliness: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a help meet for him." The Hebrew, ezer kenegdo, means a help who matches him, standing face to face.
neighbors.difference: Rama and Sita circle the fire, and Sita is given as a companion in dharma. A Jewish wedding is a covenant under the chuppah, sealed with a ring and a written ketubah of promises.
neighbors.shared: a good marriage is two people walking the same road.

neighbors.heading: matched in goodness
neighbors.text: Today Janaka called Sita Rama's companion in dharma, one who walks the right way with him. The Buddha once met an old couple, Nakula's parents, who hoped to be together in this life and the next. He told them: if a husband and wife are matched in faith, in virtue, in generosity and in wisdom, they'll see each other again.
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana, marriage is a sacred rite around the fire. The Buddha laid down no wedding rite; what joins the couple, he said, is shared goodness.
neighbors.shared: love grows strongest when two people walk toward the same good.

items.lessonTitle: the coronation planned

neighbors.heading: repel evil with good
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki said one kindness pleased Rama, and a hundred wrongs he didn't count. The Qur'an asks for the same generous memory: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend." And of the wronged: "let them forgive and show indulgence."
neighbors.difference: Valmiki shows Rama's generous memory as the sign of a great heart. The Qur'an ties forgiving others to hope in Allah's own forgiveness: forgive, as you long to be forgiven.
neighbors.shared: remember the kindness; let the hurts go uncounted.

neighbors.heading: bad is stronger than good
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki said Rama remembered one kindness and didn't count a hundred wrongs. Psychologists say most of us lean the other way. In a well-known 2001 paper, Roy Baumeister and colleagues found that bad is stronger than good: a harsh word or a hurt sticks longer than a kind one. Rama's memory runs against the grain, and that can be practiced.
neighbors.difference: For Valmiki, Rama's generous memory is part of his goodness, the heart of a dharmic king. Psychology only describes the bias, and suggests noticing good things on purpose, a habit anyone can build.
neighbors.shared: you can choose which memories you keep close.
neighbors.sources: Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer and Vohs, "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," Review of General Psychology (2001) (paraphrase)
